solution:
A body may be treated as a point object when (i) its own size is much smaller than the distance it moves in a reasonable time, and (ii) its rotation or internal motion plays no part in what is being described.

(a) Yes. The length of a carriage (a few tens of metres) is negligible compared with the distance between two stations (kilometres), and moving "without jerks" means no rotation matters.

(b) Yes. The monkey is small compared with the circumference of the track, and it does not move relative to the cycle, so the pair travels as one small object.

(c) No. The ball turns sharply precisely because it is spinning about its own axis, and the turn occurs over a distance comparable with the size of the ball. Its size and rotation are essential to the phenomenon.

(d) No. The beaker tumbles, i.e. rotates as it falls, and the height it falls through is comparable with its own size.

The body can be considered a point object in cases (a) and (b) only.

[Textbook inconsistency between the figure and the key, on part (d) only. Parts (a), (b), (c) and (e) agree with the printed key exactly. For (d) the key says A and B reach home at the SAME time, but Fig. 2.9 as printed does not show that: A's line runs on to a visibly larger \(t\) than B's before it ends at P, while B ends earlier at Q — a gap of about a quarter of the plotted time axis, far outside drawing tolerance. The answer below follows the FIGURE, because the question asks you to read the graph. Be aware that many printed solutions repeat the key's "same time", which is the answer the original drawing gave when both lines terminated together; this reprint's figure no longer does.] On an \(x\)-\(t\) graph the intercept on the \(x\)-axis is the distance of the home from the school, the intercept on the \(t\)-axis is the starting time, and the slope is the walking speed.

(a) A lives closer to the school than B, because A's line ends at P and B's at Q, and \(OP < OQ\).

(b) A starts from the school earlier than B: A's graph begins at \(t = 0\) at the origin, while B's line meets the time axis at a later instant.

(c) B walks faster than A, because B's line is steeper and the slope of an \(x\)-\(t\) graph is the velocity.

(d) A and B reach home at the different time: B reaches Q before A reaches P (B's line terminates at a smaller value of \(t\)).

(e) B overtakes A on the road once — the two lines intersect at exactly one point, and beyond it B is ahead.

Take home as the origin \(x = 0\) and the office at \(x = 2.5\,\text{km}\); take \(t\) in hours from 9.00 am.

Walking to the office: \(t = \frac{2.5\,\text{km}}{5\,\text{km h}^{-1}} = 0.5\,\text{h} = 30\,\text{min}\), so she arrives at 9.30 am.

At the office she does not move, so \(x\) stays at \(2.5\,\text{km}\) from 9.30 am to 5.00 pm.

Returning by auto: \(t = \frac{2.5\,\text{km}}{25\,\text{km h}^{-1}} = 0.1\,\text{h} = 6\,\text{min}\), so she is home at 5.06 pm.

A convenient choice of scales is 1 cm \(=\) 1 hour on the time axis and 1 cm \(=\) 0.5 km on the position axis.

The graph is therefore three straight segments joining, in order, the points

\((9.00\,\text{am},\ 0)\rightarrow(9.30\,\text{am},\ 2.5\,\text{km})\rightarrow(5.00\,\text{pm},\ 2.5\,\text{km})\rightarrow(5.06\,\text{pm},\ 0)\)

the first sloping up gently, the second horizontal (7.5 h long), the third steep and sloping down (its slope is five times as steep as the first, and negative).

Each step is \(1\,\text{m}\) and takes \(1\,\text{s}\). One complete cycle is 5 steps forward and 3 steps back: it lasts \(8\,\text{s}\) and gives a net displacement of \(+2\,\text{m}\).

So at the end of the \(n\)-th cycle, i.e. at \(t = 8n\,\text{s}\), the drunkard is at \(x = 2n\,\text{m}\). The \(x\)-\(t\) graph is a zig-zag: five unit steps up, then three unit steps down, repeating, with the whole pattern drifting steadily to the right at \(0.25\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) on average.

He does not have to complete a cycle to reach the pit — the farthest point of the \(n\)-th cycle is

\(x_{\max} = 2(n-1) + 5\)

Setting \(2(n-1) + 5 \ge 13\) gives \(n \ge 5\), so the pit is reached during the 5th cycle.

After 4 complete cycles: \(t = 32\,\text{s}\), \(x = 8\,\text{m}\). The next five steps are forward:

\(t = 33\,\text{s} \rightarrow 9\,\text{m}\), \(34 \rightarrow 10\), \(35 \rightarrow 11\), \(36 \rightarrow 12\), \(37 \rightarrow 13\,\text{m}\).

He falls into the pit \(37\,\text{s}\) after the start, having walked a total path length of \(37\,\text{m}\) for a displacement of only \(13\,\text{m}\).

Convert to SI:

\(u = 126\,\text{km h}^{-1} = 126 \times \frac{5}{18} = 35\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(v = 0\), \(x = 200\,\text{m}\)

Using \(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2ax\):

\(0 = (35)^{2} + 2a(200)\)

\(a = -\frac{1225}{400} = -3.06\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)

The negative sign means the acceleration opposes the motion, so the retardation is \(3.06\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

For the time, use \(v = u + at\):

\(t = \frac{0 - 35}{-3.0625} = 11.4\,\text{s}\)

Retardation \(= 3.06\,\text{m s}^{-2}\); time to stop \(= 11.4\,\text{s}\).

(a) The only force on the ball after it leaves the hand is gravity, so the acceleration is \(g\) directed vertically downward throughout — including during the upward motion, when it is opposite to the velocity and therefore slows the ball down.

(b) At the highest point the ball is momentarily at rest, so its velocity is \(0\), but the acceleration is still \(9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) directed vertically downward. Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration.

(c) With the origin at the highest point and the downward direction taken as positive, every point of the trajectory lies below the origin, so the position \(x\) is positive throughout. Gravity is downward, so \(a\) is positive throughout.

During the upward motion the ball moves opposite to the chosen positive direction, so \(v\) is negative: \(x > 0\), \(v < 0\), \(a > 0\).

During the downward motion it moves along the positive direction: \(x > 0\), \(v > 0\), \(a > 0\).

(d) Taking upward as positive with \(u = 29.4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(v = 0\), \(a = -9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\):

\(h = \frac{u^{2}}{2g} = \frac{(29.4)^{2}}{2 \times 9.8} = \frac{864.36}{19.6} = 44.1\,\text{m}\)

The time to rise is \(t_{up} = \frac{u}{g} = \frac{29.4}{9.8} = 3\,\text{s}\), and since the ball returns to the same level the descent takes the same time.

Height risen \(= 44.1\,\text{m}\); total time to return to the player's hands \(= 6\,\text{s}\).

(a) True. Speed is zero only at that instant; the acceleration measures how fast the velocity is changing, not how large it is. A ball thrown vertically upward has \(v = 0\) at the top of its flight while \(a = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) downward.

(b) False. Speed is defined as the magnitude of the velocity, so zero speed means the velocity vector itself is zero. The two cannot disagree at an instant.

(c) True for the one-dimensional motion the question specifies. Constant speed means \(|v|\) is fixed; in one dimension the velocity could change only by reversing sign, and since velocity varies continuously it would have to pass through zero, which would contradict the speed being constant and non-zero. So the velocity is constant and \(a = 0\). (In two or three dimensions this fails — uniform circular motion has constant speed and non-zero acceleration.)

(d) False. The sign of the acceleration depends on which direction was chosen as positive; a body speeds up only when its acceleration is along its velocity. A ball thrown upward, with the downward direction taken as positive, has \(a > 0\) while it is rising and slowing down.

Take \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and downward speeds and upward speeds both plotted as positive, since the graph asked for is a SPEED-time graph.

First fall through \(90\,\text{m}\) from rest:

\(t_{1} = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 90}{9.8}} = 4.29\,\text{s}\), and the striking speed is \(v_{1} = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{1764} = 42.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

At the collision the ball loses one tenth of its speed, so it leaves the floor at

\(v_{2} = 0.9 \times 42.0 = 37.8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

It rises, stops, and comes back to the floor in

\(\frac{2v_{2}}{g} = \frac{2 \times 37.8}{9.8} = 7.71\,\text{s}\), reaching the top of the bounce at \(t = 4.29 + 3.86 = 8.14\,\text{s}\) and the floor again at \(t = 4.29 + 7.71 = 12.0\,\text{s}\)

So the speed-time graph over \(0\) to \(12\,\text{s}\) consists of straight-line segments of slope magnitude \(9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\):

from \((0,\,0)\) rising to \((4.29\,\text{s},\ 42.0\,\text{m s}^{-1})\); a vertical drop at the impact to \(37.8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\); falling to \((8.14\,\text{s},\ 0)\) as the ball rises; rising again to \((12.0\,\text{s},\ 37.8\,\text{m s}^{-1})\) as it falls; and a second vertical drop at \(t = 12.0\,\text{s}\) to \(0.9 \times 37.8 = 34.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

The graph is thus a rising straight line, then a sequence of \(\vee\)-shaped arcs of decreasing height, with a sudden drop in speed at each bounce.
_note: The stem gives no value of g. 9.8 m s^-2 is used because it is the value the chapter itself adopts for free fall AND because it makes the numbers exact: sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 90) = 42.0 m s^-1 exactly, and the second collision then falls exactly on t = 12.0 s, the end of the interval the question asks for. With g = 10 the second impact would land at 11.88 s, which does not.

solution:
(a) The magnitude of the displacement over an interval is \(|x_{2} - x_{1}|\), the length of the straight line from the initial to the final position — it depends only on the two end points. The total path length is the whole distance actually covered along the path.

Example: a particle goes from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 5\,\text{m}\) and returns to \(x = 0\). The magnitude of the displacement is \(0\); the path length is \(10\,\text{m}\).

Dividing the interval into small sub-intervals, the total displacement is the sum \(\sum \Delta x_{i}\) of the signed sub-displacements while the path length is \(\sum |\Delta x_{i}|\). Since

\(\left|\sum \Delta x_{i}\right| \le \sum \left|\Delta x_{i}\right|\)

the path length is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of the displacement.

(b) Dividing both quantities in (a) by the same time interval \(\Delta t\) gives

magnitude of average velocity \(= \frac{|\text{displacement}|}{\Delta t}\)  and  average speed \(= \frac{\text{path length}}{\Delta t}\)

so the same inequality carries over: average speed \(\ge\) magnitude of average velocity.

In the example above the magnitude of the average velocity is zero while the average speed is not.

Equality holds in both (a) and (b) exactly when the particle does not reverse its direction at any instant of the interval, i.e. the motion is along a straight line in one direction only. Then every \(\Delta x_{i}\) has the same sign and the two sums coincide.

Time to reach the market \(= \frac{2.5\,\text{km}}{5\,\text{km h}^{-1}} = 0.5\,\text{h} = 30\,\text{min}\); time to walk back \(= \frac{2.5\,\text{km}}{7.5\,\text{km h}^{-1}} = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{h} = 20\,\text{min}\). The round trip therefore takes \(50\,\text{min}\).

(i) 0 to 30 min: he is just at the market, displacement \(= 2.5\,\text{km}\), path length \(= 2.5\,\text{km}\).

magnitude of average velocity \(= \frac{2.5}{0.5} = 5\,\text{km h}^{-1}\); average speed \(= 5\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)

(ii) 0 to 50 min: he is back home, displacement \(= 0\), path length \(= 5\,\text{km}\).

magnitude of average velocity \(= 0\); average speed \(= \frac{5}{50/60} = 6\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)

(iii) 0 to 40 min: he left the market at 30 min and has been returning for 10 min, covering \(7.5 \times \frac{10}{60} = 1.25\,\text{km}\). He is therefore \(2.5 - 1.25 = 1.25\,\text{km}\) from home, having walked \(2.5 + 1.25 = 3.75\,\text{km}\).

magnitude of average velocity \(= \frac{1.25}{40/60} = 1.875\,\text{km h}^{-1}\); average speed \(= \frac{3.75}{40/60} = 5.625\,\text{km h}^{-1}\)

Summary — magnitude of average velocity: (i) \(5\,\text{km h}^{-1}\), (ii) \(0\), (iii) \(1.875\,\text{km h}^{-1}\); average speed: (i) \(5\,\text{km h}^{-1}\), (ii) \(6\,\text{km h}^{-1}\), (iii) \(5.625\,\text{km h}^{-1}\).

Over a finite interval the average speed can exceed the magnitude of the average velocity only because the particle may reverse its direction inside the interval, which makes the path length longer than the net displacement.

Instantaneous quantities are limits as \(\Delta t \to 0\). In a vanishingly small interval the particle has no opportunity to turn round: the small piece of path it covers coincides with the straight-line displacement, so

\(\Delta s \to |\Delta x|\)  as  \(\Delta t \to 0\)

Dividing by \(\Delta t\) and taking the limit,

\(\text{instantaneous speed} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{|\Delta x|}{\Delta t} = \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\)

So the instantaneous speed is always exactly the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, and no separate definition is needed.

Every one of the four graphs is impossible, each for its own reason. The common thread is that position, velocity, speed and path length are all single-valued functions of time, and speed and path length carry extra restrictions of their own.

(a) The \(x\)-\(t\) curve loops back on itself, so it gives the particle two different positions at the same instant. A particle cannot be in two places at once.

(b) The \(v\)-\(t\) curve is a closed loop, so it gives two different velocities at the same instant. A particle cannot have two velocities at once.

(c) The graph shows negative speed. Speed is the magnitude of the velocity and can never be negative.

(d) The total path length is shown decreasing over part of the graph. Path length is the total distance covered so far, which can only increase or stay the same as time goes on; it can never decrease.

None of the four graphs can represent one-dimensional motion of a particle.

No, it is not correct. The graph is an \(x\)-\(t\) plot, not a picture of the path. It shows how one coordinate varies with time; the question already states that the motion is one-dimensional, so the particle travels along a straight line for all \(t\), both before and after \(t = 0\). The shape of the curve tells us about the velocity and acceleration, not about the geometry of the trajectory: the flat part means the particle is at rest, and the upward-curving part means it is moving with increasing speed, i.e. accelerating.

A suitable physical context is a body that is at rest until \(t = 0\) and then starts to move from rest along a straight line with uniform acceleration, so that \(x = \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\) for \(t > 0\).

For example: a stone held at rest and released at \(t = 0\), falling freely, with \(x\) measured vertically downward from the point of release; or a car standing at a traffic signal which starts off with uniform acceleration the moment the light turns green.

The muzzle speed is the speed of the bullet relative to the gun, and the gun is carried by the moving van, so the bullet's speed relative to the ground is the muzzle speed plus the van's speed. What damages the thief's car is the speed of the bullet relative to that car.

Convert to SI:

\(v_{\text{van}} = 30\,\text{km h}^{-1} = 30 \times \frac{5}{18} = 8.33\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(v_{\text{thief}} = 192\,\text{km h}^{-1} = 192 \times \frac{5}{18} = 53.33\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Speed of the bullet relative to the ground:

\(v_{b} = 150 + 8.33 = 158.33\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Both move in the same direction, so the relative speed is the difference:

\(v_{b} - v_{\text{thief}} = 158.33 - 53.33 = 105\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

The bullet hits the thief's car with a speed of \(105\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

(a) The \(x\)-\(t\) graph shows a body at rest, then moving in the positive direction with constant velocity up to A, then suddenly reversing and moving in the negative direction with a smaller constant speed until it comes to rest again at a negative position. A situation that fits: a ball lying at rest on a smooth floor is kicked towards a wall; it rebounds from the wall at A with reduced speed, travels back past its starting point, and is finally stopped by a second wall.

(b) The \(v\)-\(t\) graph is a set of straight segments of the same negative slope, each starting at a positive velocity and ending at a negative one, with the velocity jumping abruptly at regular instants and the magnitudes shrinking each time. The constant negative slope is \(-g\), and the sudden jumps are collisions. This is a ball thrown vertically upwards which bounces repeatedly off the floor, losing speed at every bounce.

(c) The acceleration is zero except for a single short, large pulse. This is a body moving uniformly that receives a brief, strong force — for example a cricket ball travelling at constant velocity that is struck by a bat for a very short time and sent back.

In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is \(a = -\omega^{2}x\), so the acceleration always has the sign OPPOSITE to the displacement. The velocity is the slope of the \(x\)-\(t\) curve.

At \(t = 0.3\,\text{s}\): the curve lies below the time axis and is still falling towards the minimum that follows, so

\(x < 0\), \(v < 0\), \(a > 0\)

At \(t = 1.2\,\text{s}\): the curve lies above the time axis and is still rising towards the maximum that follows, so

\(x > 0\), \(v > 0\), \(a < 0\)

At \(t = -1.2\,\text{s}\): the curve lies below the time axis but has just passed its minimum and is rising, so

\(x < 0\), \(v > 0\), \(a > 0\)

In each case the sign of \(a\) is simply the opposite of the sign of \(x\), as it must be for simple harmonic motion.

For an \(x\)-\(t\) graph the average velocity over an interval is the slope of the chord joining its end points, and since the three intervals are equal in duration, comparing average speeds is the same as comparing the magnitudes of the changes in \(x\).

Interval 3 spans the steeply falling part of the curve, where \(|\Delta x|\) is by far the largest, so the average speed is greatest in interval 3.

Interval 2 straddles the maximum of the curve, where the graph is almost flat; \(|\Delta x|\) there is the smallest of the three, so the average speed is least in interval 2.

Signs of the average velocity: in interval 1 the curve rises, so it is positive; in interval 2 the curve ends slightly higher than it began, so it is positive (but very small); in interval 3 the curve falls steeply, so it is negative.

Average speed: greatest in interval 3, least in interval 2. Average velocity: positive in intervals 1 and 2, negative in interval 3.

On a speed-time graph the average acceleration over an interval is the slope of the chord joining its end points, and the instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the tangent.

Average acceleration greatest in magnitude: interval 2. The three intervals are equal in duration, and in interval 2 the curve drops steeply from just after B, giving much the largest change of speed.

Average speed greatest: interval 3. That interval sits at the peak D, where the speed itself is highest, so the mean of the speed over the interval is the largest.

Signs: the particle moves along a constant direction, which has been chosen as positive, so \(v > 0\) in all three intervals. For the acceleration, the speed is increasing in interval 1 so \(a > 0\); it is decreasing in interval 2 so \(a < 0\); in interval 3 the speed is still marginally higher at the end than at the start, so \(a > 0\), but the interval lies almost astride the maximum D and the increase is very small.

At the points A, B, C and D the tangent to the speed-time curve is parallel to the time axis — A lies on the initial flat portion, B and D are maxima, and C is a minimum. The slope is zero at each, so the acceleration is zero at all four points.
